stories.headline: India's West Asia oil imports return to pre-war levels in September
stories.title: India's West Asia oil imports return to pre-war levels in September
stories.summary: Refiners snapped up spot cargoes as West Asian producers and traders cranked up shipments through the Strait ‌of ⁠Hormuz, easing supply constraints caused by the Iran war
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: India's imports of West Asian crude oil surged in September, returning to pre-war levels, while its refiners cut back purchases of Russian oil amid stiff competition with China, ship tracking data showed.
Refiners snapped up spot cargoes as West Asian producers and traders cranked up shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, easing supply constraints caused by the Iran war.
The world's third-biggest oil importer initially raised Russian crude imports to compensate for reduced West Asian supplies at the onset of the war.
India's crude imports from West Asia jumped in September to about 2.8 million barrels per day, the highest since February, up from 32 per cent in August, the data showed.
Gulf oil accounted for about 54 per cent of overall imports.

In contrast, Russian oil imports fell about 14 per cent on month to about 1.8 million bpd in September, with its share of India's oil purchases declining to 33.5 per cent from 46.6 per cent, the data showed.

Russian oil purchases by Indian refiners are likely to remain subdued in the coming months as the landed cost of Russian oil is now comparable to that of some West Asian grades, mainly Iraqi oil, said an Indian refining source.
Premiums on Russian oil have narrowed to $1-$2 per barrel against Brent from over $10 in recent months as West Asian supplies hit markets, the source said.

Refiners would prefer to maximise purchases of discounted West Asian crude because voyage times are shorter and some producers have cut selling prices to offset soaring freight costs, the source added.
"We will buy from whoever offers us better prices," said this source.
India's overall imports in September rose 20 per cent month-on-month to around 5.33 million bpd, the data showed.
Russia remained India's largest oil supplier, followed by the United Arab Emirates and Iraq, the data showed.

stories.headline: India backs continuation of UN war crimes tribunal mechanism
stories.title: India backs continuation of UN war crimes tribunal mechanism
stories.summary: India has backed the continuation of the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals (IRMCT), stressing that its residual functions remain vital for protecting victims and witnesses, preserving tribunal archives, and ensuring accountability for war crimes and genocide in Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: India has backed the continuation of the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals (IRMCT), stressing that its residual functions remain vital for protecting victims and witnesses, preserving tribunal archives, and ensuring accountability for war crimes and genocide in Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia.

United Nations: India backs keeping the mechanism established to continue the work of two international criminal tribunals, saying this would ensure continued accountability for the war crimes and genocide committed in the two regions.

“India underscores the importance of the mechanism continuing residual functions, including the protection of victims and witnesses, assistance to national jurisdictions, and the preservation and management of the tribunal’s archives”, Congress MP Manish Tiwari said on Wednesday (local time).
“These functions remain essential to safeguarding the legacy of the ad hoc tribunals and ensuring continued accountability”, he said.

He was speaking at a plenary session of the General Assembly on the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals (IRMCT), which was set up by the Security Council in 2010 to take on the unfinished work of the International Criminal Tribunals for Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia.

The Rwanda tribunal tried those responsible for the genocide of the Tutsis during a civil war and ended its work in 1994, while the Yugoslav tribunal that rendered justice on war crimes closed in 1993.
The Yugoslav tribunal held 111 trials and convicted 90 persons, one of whom has an appeal pending with the IRMCT.
The Rwanda tribunal indicted 86 persons in connection with the genocide of about 800,000 Tutsi ethnic group and some moderate Hutus by the Hutu extremists who controlled the government of Rwanda.
The IRMCT convicted 61 people after it picked up some of the cases from the tribunal.

“We recognise the mechanism’s contribution to the fight against impunity and reiterate the importance of fulfilling its mandate in accordance with the principles of justice, impartiality, fairness and due process, upholding the interests of justice and protecting the rights of victims remains essential”, Tiwari said.

As the IRMCT “moves towards completing its mandate, we emphasise the need for an efficient, orderly and time-bound transition without compromising judicial independence or the effective discharge of its remaining responsibilities”, he said.

stories.headline: Ukraine's strikes on Russian data centres disrupt key services, derail AI research
stories.title: Ukraine's strikes on Russian data centres disrupt key services, derail AI research
stories.summary: Moscow, Oct 22: Russia prides itself on its digital advances -- from an extensive e-commerce services sector to ambitious plans for developing artificial intelligence. But now, some of the key data centres at the heart of its technical prowess have been knocked out by Ukrainian drone attacks in the 4.5-year-old full-scale invasion, suffering damage that could take a long time to repair. Ukraine this month hit three main data centres belonging to tech giant Yandex, one for Russia's biggest bank, Sberbank, and one for social media platform VKontakte, the country's equivalent to Facebook. While Yandex, Sberbank and VKontakte are coy about the damage, people and businesses across Russia have reported widespread interruptions to cloud services. Banking, e-commerce, geolocation and ride-hailing services, as well as Alisa, Yandex's virtual assistant, and multimodal AI chatbots all have suffered lasting disruptions. The fallout even spread to Russia's judicial system, reportedly forcing arbitration courts to cancel or postpone sessions and cutting database access. Most experts predict repairing the damage could take months, if not years. Some warn that Moscow's aspirations to become a leader in AI development could be significantly set back. “This effectively sets Russia far behind in the AI race,” said Mikhail Klimarev, head of the Internet Protection Society activist group. Data centres have been hit by both sides in the war Data centres are the latest targets of aerial campaigns waged by both sides against each other's vital infrastructure. Russian missiles and drones have pummelled Ukraine's power grid and other key sites, part of Kremlin efforts to weaken morale and resistance. Moscow stepped up those attacks as winter approaches, taking advantage of a shortage of US-supplied Patriot interceptors, whose stockpiles have been drained by Washington's war with Iran. Ukraine retaliated with waves of drone attacks against Russian oil refineries, triggering a massive fuel crisis and bringing the war home to millions of civilians. US President Donald Trump has blamed the attacks for higher global oil prices, which have escalated largely due to the US war in Iran. Earlier this month, Trump struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin to import diesel oil, shocking Ukraine and its allies. Ukraine also hit huge warehouses for Russia's top online retailers, Wildberries and Ozon. Kyiv's attacks on Russian data centres closely followed Moscow's recent strikes on data centres in Ukraine, which disrupted the internet and TV broadcasts. On October 8, Ukrainian drones hit a Yandex data centre in Sasovo in the Ryazan region that houses two of the company's three supercomputers. A data centre in Kaluga was hit a day later and the one in Vladimir was struck October 11. The data centre and AI hub for Sberbank was hit October 14 in Balakovo in the Saratov region, and four days later, Kyiv struck a data centre in St. Petersburg serving VKontakte. Data centres are vulnerable While oil refineries and warehouses are easy prey, data centres are even softer targets -- massive buildings packed with servers and supporting power and cooling infrastructure. Lasting damage can result from a drone carrying a relatively light load of explosives. The vulnerability of data centres was exposed by Iran, whose drones hit two Amazon Web Services data centres in the United Arab Emirates and one in Bahrain. AWS said last month it was unable to restore access to the resources and data hosted at two of them. Yandex has run drills for an accident that could incapacitate one of its six data centres, but it was caught unprepared when its three key facilities were hit over four days. It wasn't immediately clear why air defences near the sites had failed. “The problem in Russia is that they've got to cover a big country with air defence and they don't have enough,” said Nick Reiners, senior geotechnology analyst at Eurasia Group. Russia's efforts to build a sovereign internet backfire Ukraine has stored critical data on servers in allied European countries, helping limit the damage from Russian attacks. But Moscow's strict digital sovereignty policy requires all data storage at home, making it extremely vulnerable. “Because all the infrastructure and all the data is located inside Russia, it's relatively easier to take down,” Reiners said. Klimarev predicted the data centre attacks could encourage many top Russian companies to move data abroad, while the authorities could ease their efforts to tighten internet controls to minimise the damage. “Paradoxically, the strikes on data centres have saved the Russian internet from isolation, as they will now have to move computing assets, most likely, to Europe,” Klimarev said. “It's quite likely that many Russian businesses are now roaming the European market to rent computing assets.” Russians are vexed by service disruptions Yandex dominates digital life in Russia and many former Soviet nations. It provides a wide variety of functions, including a search engine, cloud storage, payment apps, geolocation and ride-hailing services, and e-commerce platforms. “Yandex is kind of like Uber and Amazon and Google and everything rolled into one,” with everything "concentrated in just a few data centres,” Reiners said. “From a strategic perspective, they're an excellent target.” The attacks on Yandex caused unprecedented disruptions, paralysing payments, online orders, taxi rides and access to personal data. Moscow resident Igor Mann said he couldn't collect an order he placed with Yandex Market, an e-commerce platform. He said he tried using a virtual private network, but “nothing worked.” Taxi driver Pavel Belyavskiy, who gets orders via Yandex's ride-hailing app, couldn't connect with passengers. “On several orders already, I've ended up waiting for a long time and had to cancel the ride because I couldn't even get in touch with the passenger,” he said. The attacks also caused temporary disruptions at some major companies and banks that rely on Yandex cloud services. “It's not just about convenience -- it's also about work ... tied to everyday life,” said another Moscow resident, Eduard Malyavko. A blow to Russia's AI ambitions Yandex said it restored most key cloud services in the following days as it turned to other data centres in Russia. But the damage to the company's AI development efforts is widely seen as massive and longer-lasting. Yandex has invested in huge data centres as the global AI boom fuels demand for computing power. The company's three supercomputers used to develop models are ranked among the top 500 in the world. Its most powerful computer -- at the Sasovo data centre -- was ranked 19th. Yandex didn't disclose the extent of the strikes' consequences, but satellite images indicated its data centres sustained serious damage. Some observers noted that fires triggered by the attacks probably seriously damaged high-end chips and other key equipment. “With this kind of hit, it's hard to expect that at least something was left intact -- the data centres' equipment is fragile, demanding and expensive,” Klimarev said. “Soot from the fire is bad for electronics.” While Russia already lagged years behind the US and China, “Ukraine's drone strikes will likely still set back Russian AI efforts further,” said Connor Martin, an expert with the Council for Foreign Relations. He said in a commentary that Russia likely will struggle to quickly replace the US-designed Nvidia A100 chips powering Yandex's supercomputers. Klimarev also said the global deficit of high-end chips, combined with the sanctions on their delivery to Russia, will make repairs long and costly. “I'm not sure it can be done in half a year, a year, or even at all,” he said.

stories.headline: The Darkest Day in the History of Jammu & Kashmir
stories.title: The Darkest Day in the History of Jammu & Kashmir
stories.summary: CROSS ROADS No single event has shaped the uncertainty of the future that the people of Jammu & Kashmir (J&K) uncomfortably and hesitantly peek out towards than those that unfolded on 22 October 1947. In the din of the cacophony of voices parroting ad nauseam terms such as the Line of Control (LoC), the United Nations (UN) Resolutions on J&K, the Shimla Agreement, statehood for Gilgit Baltistan, Article 370 of India’s Constitution, and the like, the reason why these terms came into being in the first place has sadly long ceased to be a matter of interest to a vast majority of even those that deliberate publicly and vociferously on the plight of J&K. On that very day the seeds were sown for the physical tearing apart of J&K, for what we see today as the blurring of the identity of J&K and its people, for the destruction of the peaceful and inclusive way of life in the region and the crumbling of the long-held social values in J&K, and for the induction of the ugly head of terrorism into J&K by Pakistan. In essence, the roots of the hydra-headed predicament that J&K confronts today can indubitably be traced back to that one single event that commenced on that fateful autumn day. As gripping and intriguing as the history of the region in the period leading up to, and in the aftermath of, the events of October 1947 were, for the purpose of this piece, I shall restrict it to sketching the broad outlines. Maharaja Hari Singh, the Hindu Dogra ruler of Muslim-majority J&K at the time of India’s independence, seemed inclined towards independence and did not initially appear to be keen to join either dominion. On 12 August 1947, he therefore sought a standstill agreement with both India and Pakistan. He communicated to both that the “Jammu and Kashmir government would welcome standstill agreement with Union of India/Pakistan on all matters on which there exists arrangements with the outgoing British India government”. India responded by asking Maharaja Hari Singh to send his representative to Delhi for further discussions. J&K did not send a representative to Delhi, and no negotiations were consequently held. Pakistan, on the other hand, accepted the J&K offer of a standstill agreement and on 15 August 1947 sent a communication to Janak Singh, the then Prime Minister of J&K, confirming the same. Pakistan, however, made its nefarious designs on J&K clear when within 12 days of agreeing to the standstill agreement, on 24 August 1947 it threatened Maharaja Hari Singh by writing to him that “The time has come for Maharaja of Kashmir that he must take his choice and choose Pakistan. Should Kashmir fail to join Pakistan, the gravest possible trouble will inevitably ensue”. These turned out to be ominous words indeed, as from that day onwards and continuing onto the present day, Pakistan’s consistent policy has actually been to incessantly and ruthlessly stir up the “gravest possible trouble” in J&K. By end-August 1947, suspecting that Maharaja Hari Singh may accede to India and apprehensive of the popular J&K leader Sheikh Abdullah’s dim view of Pakistan, Pakistan had already decided to seize J&K by force. The then Pakistani military officer in charge of Kashmir, Major General Akbar Khan, had aptly summarized the thinking in the Pakistani establishment when he wrote, “Kashmir’s accession to Pakistan was not simply a matter of desirability but of absolute necessity for its separate existence”. On 4 September 1947, General Henry Lawrence Scott, commander of the Jammu and Kashmir State forces, complained about multiple covert incursions from Pakistan and asked the Maharaja’s government to raise this issue with Pakistan. In his autobiography, Dr. Karan Singh, the son of Maharaja Hari Singh and the heir apparent of J&K, wrote, “Intelligence reports from the frontier areas of Poonch and Mirpur as well as the Sialkot sector started coming in which spoke of large-scale massacre, loot and rape of our villagers by aggressive hordes from across the borders. I recall the grim atmosphere that began to engulf us as it gradually became clear that we were losing control of the outer areas”. Operation Gulmarg had been conceived and put into action as early as on 20 August 1947, just six days after Pakistan was carved out from British India. The plan, as openly reported since, was for Pashtun tribes of Pakistan’s North-West Frontier Province (NWFP) to enlist at least one Lashkar of 1000 tribesmen each. Separate instructions for their recruitment were issued to the Deputy Commissioners and Political Agents of NWFP. After enlistment, these Lashkars were to be concentrated at Bannu, Wana, Peshawar, Kohat, Thal and Nowshera by the first week of September 1947. The Pakistan Army Brigade Commanders at these places were to issue them arms and ammunition. The Pakistani Army superimposed a Pathan Major, a Captain and ten JCOs of the regular Pakistan Army above each such armed Lashkar, and these Army regulars were required to dress and live exactly like the other Pathans in the Lashkar. The entire force was commanded by Major General Akbar Khan, code named General Tariq, who was assisted by Brigadier Sher Khan. Among those who planned, led, and financed Operation Gulmarg, the most prominent was Sardar Shaukat Hayat Khan, a close confidant of Pakistan’s founder Muhammad Ali Jinnah and a top leader of the Muslim League. In his book ‘The Nation that Lost its Soul’, Shaukat Hayat Khan acknowledged that he had been appointed supervisor of the Kashmir operation (P.278), and that Major Khurshid Anwar was given the responsibility of contacting the chiefs of the Pathan tribes to enlist the tribal militants. He also disclosed that three hundred thousand rupees were given from the Pakistan treasury by Finance Minister Ghulam Muhammad for this operation. Major General Akbar Khan fixed 22 October 1947 as the date on which the attack on J&K would be launched. All the Lashkars were asked to converge at Abbottabad near the border with J&K by 18 October. They were moved in civil buses and trucks that had been commandeered for this purpose, and all their movement took place under the cover of night. The tribal militants assembled in a separate area 16 km outside Abbottabad that had been prepared for them. Infantry Divisions of the Pakistani Army also descended on the Murree-Abbottabad and other key areas with instructions to move in quickly into J&K to back up the Lashkars and consolidate their hold over captured territory. Operation Gulmarg was launched on the intervening night of 21-22 October 1947. Over 2,000 Pathan tribesmen first captured the bridge spanning the Kishanganga (Neelam) River on the Hazara Trunk Road linking Muzaffarabad with Abbottabad without a fight. The J&K troops guarding the bridge deserted and joined the attacking tribesmen. By morning, the first major J&K border town of Muzaffarabad had been captured. The horrors that then unfolded in Muzaffarabad were chronicled by Pakistani journalist Zahid Chaudhry in his 12-volume work 'Pakistan ki siyasi tarikh' (Political History of Pakistan). Chaudhry wrote that for three days the invaders indulged in killing non-Muslims, looting, plundering and burning their houses. A large number of women were raped and kidnapped. As the officer in-charge of the attack, Major Khurshid Anwar encouraged the killing, loot, arson, rape and kidnapping of non-Muslims that took place. Writers and commentators have estimated the number of the Hindus and Sikhs massacred during these three days in Muzaffarabad to be 4500 to 5000, and the number of kidnapped women to be more than 1600. Pakistan has perpetuated the myth that the tribal raiders were liberators and came to Kashmir to fulfil their religious obligation of Jihad because Muslims were being killed in Jammu in communal riots. However, the reality was that it was not as if Muslims had been spared. Thousands of Kashmiri Muslims were also killed by the marauding tribesmen. As an eyewitness account of Khawaja Abdul Samad asserted, “their attack had totally devastated Muzaffarabad, the homes of Hindus and Muslims were looted, shops were plundered, places of worships were not spared; they tore down Mandirs and desecrated Masjids”. Zahid Chaudhry pointed out that the Afridi and Mahsud Lashkars did not participate in the invasion of J&K out of any religious consideration, and their primary aim was loot and plunder and the kidnapping of women. Gohar Rahman of Battagram, 80 km north-west of Garhi Habibullah in Pakistan, who had participated in the invasion and had returned to Garhi Habibullah along with many other tribesmen when the first winter snows came, later told the BBC that the tribal militants had “returned with war booty”. He elaborated that “Some had brought cattle, some horses. Most of them had brought arms, and many brought women. One Afridi tribesman walked back with two women in tow. They wept incessantly and just wouldn't stop”. The Pakistan Army then directed the Lashkars to Mirpur, after capturing which they moved on to take Uri before reaching the vibrant and important town of Baramulla, about 50 kms west of Srinagar, on 26 October. The mayhem of killings, rapes and plunder was repeated at every stop along the route, while other Lashkars that had been sent through other routes with different targets in J&K did not account for themselves any better. Baramulla, however, represented another major town that bore the brunt of the ruthless ways of the tribal militants. On 26 October 1947 alone, the intruders massacred about eleven thousand residents of Baramulla and destroyed the Mohra power station. Estimates of the total number of residents of J&K killed in the tribal invasion range between 35,000 to 40,000. opening: CROSS ROADS No single event has shaped the uncertainty of the future that the people of Jammu & Kashmir (J&K) uncomfortably and hesitantly peek out towards than those that unfolded on 22 October 1947.

In the din of the cacophony of voices parroting ad nauseam terms such as the Line of Control (LoC), the United Nations (UN) Resolutions on J&K, the Shimla Agreement, statehood for Gilgit Baltistan, Article 370 of India’s Constitution, and the like, the reason why these terms came into being in the first place has sadly long ceased to be a matter of interest to a vast majority of even those that deliberate publicly and vociferously on the plight of J&K. On that very day the seeds were sown for the physical tearing apart of J&K, for what we see today as the blurring of the identity of J&K and its people, for the destruction of the peaceful and inclusive way of life in the region and the crumbling of the long-held social values in J&K, and for the induction of the ugly head of terrorism into J&K by Pakistan.
body: In essence, the roots of the hydra-headed predicament that J&K confronts today can indubitably be traced back to that one single event that commenced on that fateful autumn day.

As gripping and intriguing as the history of the region in the period leading up to, and in the aftermath of, the events of October 1947 were, for the purpose of this piece, I shall restrict it to sketching the broad outlines.

Maharaja Hari Singh, the Hindu Dogra ruler of Muslim-majority J&K at the time of India’s independence, seemed inclined towards independence and did not initially appear to be keen to join either dominion.
On 12 August 1947, he therefore sought a standstill agreement with both India and Pakistan.

He communicated to both that the “Jammu and Kashmir government would welcome standstill agreement with Union of India/Pakistan on all matters on which there exists arrangements with the outgoing British India government”.
India responded by asking Maharaja Hari Singh to send his representative to Delhi for further discussions.
J&K did not send a representative to Delhi, and no negotiations were consequently held.
Pakistan, on the other hand, accepted the J&K offer of a standstill agreement and on 15 August 1947 sent a communication to Janak Singh, the then Prime Minister of J&K, confirming the same.

Pakistan, however, made its nefarious designs on J&K clear when within 12 days of agreeing to the standstill agreement, on 24 August 1947 it threatened Maharaja Hari Singh by writing to him that “The time has come for Maharaja of Kashmir that he must take his choice and choose Pakistan.
Should Kashmir fail to join Pakistan, the gravest possible trouble will inevitably ensue”.

These turned out to be ominous words indeed, as from that day onwards and continuing onto the present day, Pakistan’s consistent policy has actually been to incessantly and ruthlessly stir up the “gravest possible trouble” in J&K. By end-August 1947, suspecting that Maharaja Hari Singh may accede to India and apprehensive of the popular J&K leader Sheikh Abdullah’s dim view of Pakistan, Pakistan had already decided to seize J&K by force.

The then Pakistani military officer in charge of Kashmir, Major General Akbar Khan, had aptly summarized the thinking in the Pakistani establishment when he wrote, “Kashmir’s accession to Pakistan was not simply a matter of desirability but of absolute necessity for its separate existence”.

On 4 September 1947, General Henry Lawrence Scott, commander of the Jammu and Kashmir State forces, complained about multiple covert incursions from Pakistan and asked the Maharaja’s government to raise this issue with Pakistan.

In his autobiography, Dr. Karan Singh, the son of Maharaja Hari Singh and the heir apparent of J&K, wrote, “Intelligence reports from the frontier areas of Poonch and Mirpur as well as the Sialkot sector started coming in which spoke of large-scale massacre, loot and rape of our villagers by aggressive hordes from across the borders.
I recall the grim atmosphere that began to engulf us as it gradually became clear that we were losing control of the outer areas”.
Operation Gulmarg had been conceived and put into action as early as on 20 August 1947, just six days after Pakistan was carved out from British India.
The plan, as openly reported since, was for Pashtun tribes of Pakistan’s North-West Frontier Province (NWFP) to enlist at least one Lashkar of 1000 tribesmen each.
Separate instructions for their recruitment were issued to the Deputy Commissioners and Political Agents of NWFP.
After enlistment, these Lashkars were to be concentrated at Bannu, Wana, Peshawar, Kohat, Thal and Nowshera by the first week of September 1947.
The Pakistan Army Brigade Commanders at these places were to issue them arms and ammunition.

The Pakistani Army superimposed a Pathan Major, a Captain and ten JCOs of the regular Pakistan Army above each such armed Lashkar, and these Army regulars were required to dress and live exactly like the other Pathans in the Lashkar.
The entire force was commanded by Major General Akbar Khan, code named General Tariq, who was assisted by Brigadier Sher Khan.

Among those who planned, led, and financed Operation Gulmarg, the most prominent was Sardar Shaukat Hayat Khan, a close confidant of Pakistan’s founder Muhammad Ali Jinnah and a top leader of the Muslim League.

In his book ‘The Nation that Lost its Soul’, Shaukat Hayat Khan acknowledged that he had been appointed supervisor of the Kashmir operation (P.278), and that Major Khurshid Anwar was given the responsibility of contacting the chiefs of the Pathan tribes to enlist the tribal militants.
He also disclosed that three hundred thousand rupees were given from the Pakistan treasury by Finance Minister Ghulam Muhammad for this operation.
Major General Akbar Khan fixed 22 October 1947 as the date on which the attack on J&K would be launched.
All the Lashkars were asked to converge at Abbottabad near the border with J&K by 18 October.
They were moved in civil buses and trucks that had been commandeered for this purpose, and all their movement took place under the cover of night.
The tribal militants assembled in a separate area 16 km outside Abbottabad that had been prepared for them.

Infantry Divisions of the Pakistani Army also descended on the Murree-Abbottabad and other key areas with instructions to move in quickly into J&K to back up the Lashkars and consolidate their hold over captured territory.
Operation Gulmarg was launched on the intervening night of 21-22 October 1947.
Over 2,000 Pathan tribesmen first captured the bridge spanning the Kishanganga (Neelam) River on the Hazara Trunk Road linking Muzaffarabad with Abbottabad without a fight.
The J&K troops guarding the bridge deserted and joined the attacking tribesmen.
By morning, the first major J&K border town of Muzaffarabad had been captured.
The horrors that then unfolded in Muzaffarabad were chronicled by Pakistani journalist Zahid Chaudhry in his 12-volume work 'Pakistan ki siyasi tarikh' (Political History of Pakistan).
Chaudhry wrote that for three days the invaders indulged in killing non-Muslims, looting, plundering and burning their houses.
A large number of women were raped and kidnapped.
As the officer in-charge of the attack, Major Khurshid Anwar encouraged the killing, loot, arson, rape and kidnapping of non-Muslims that took place.

Writers and commentators have estimated the number of the Hindus and Sikhs massacred during these three days in Muzaffarabad to be 4500 to 5000, and the number of kidnapped women to be more than 1600.

Pakistan has perpetuated the myth that the tribal raiders were liberators and came to Kashmir to fulfil their religious obligation of Jihad because Muslims were being killed in Jammu in communal riots.
However, the reality was that it was not as if Muslims had been spared.
Thousands of Kashmiri Muslims were also killed by the marauding tribesmen.

As an eyewitness account of Khawaja Abdul Samad asserted, “their attack had totally devastated Muzaffarabad, the homes of Hindus and Muslims were looted, shops were plundered, places of worships were not spared; they tore down Mandirs and desecrated Masjids”.

Zahid Chaudhry pointed out that the Afridi and Mahsud Lashkars did not participate in the invasion of J&K out of any religious consideration, and their primary aim was loot and plunder and the kidnapping of women.
He elaborated that “Some had brought cattle, some horses.
Most of them had brought arms, and many brought women.
One Afridi tribesman walked back with two women in tow.
They wept incessantly and just wouldn't stop”.

The Pakistan Army then directed the Lashkars to Mirpur, after capturing which they moved on to take Uri before reaching the vibrant and important town of Baramulla, about 50 kms west of Srinagar, on 26 October.

The mayhem of killings, rapes and plunder was repeated at every stop along the route, while other Lashkars that had been sent through other routes with different targets in J&K did not account for themselves any better.

stories.headline: Ladakh makes judicial history
stories.title: Ladakh makes judicial history
stories.summary: Leh, Oct 21: A historic chapter in the Indian judicial history unfolded on Wednesday when Chief Justice of the High Court of J&K and Ladakh, Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice Sanjay Parihar presided over the first regular division bench at Leh. The newly established Ladakh Bench of the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh located at a breath-taking height of over 11,500 feet above sea level, began regular hearing of the cases from Wednesday. The day began with the hearing by the Division Bench in which the Chief Justice heard the matters through virtual mode while Justice Sanjay Parihar was present physically at the Ladakh Bench. After the conclusion of the hearing of five listed Division Bench matters, Justice Sanjay Parihar sat singly and dealt with as many as 60 matters listed before the single bench. Today’s proceedings made use of technology to facilitate a sort of hybrid hearing with the Chief Justice hearing through virtual mode and Justice Sanjay Parihar doing physical hearing. Justice Parihar said that the identification of the 65 cases that were listed today reflects the initial effort to organise and facilitate the hearing of matters concerning litigants from Ladakh. He said that the successful commencement of regular judicial hearings today by the Chief Justice in such a high-altitude location is a landmark achievement in the country’s judicial infrastructure and commitment to ensuring that geographical barriers do not become obstacles to justice. The establishment of the Ladakh Bench is a significant step in strengthening the reach of constitutional institutions to remote and geographically challenging regions of the country. Earlier, litigants from Leh, Kargil, and other far-flung areas of Ladakh would undertake lengthy journeys to Srinagar or Jammu for proceedings before the High Court. The commencement of hearings here is also encouraging for the legal fraternity of Ladakh including advocates. Ladakh Bench of J& K High court was formally inaugurated by the Chief Justice of India Justice Surya Kant on October 18 at Melongthang, Leh.

stories.headline: INDIA bloc leaders to hold virtual meeting, roadmap for 'vote chori' protests on agenda
stories.title: INDIA bloc leaders to hold virtual meeting, roadmap for 'vote chori' protests on agenda
stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 22: An virtual meeting of the INDIA bloc will be held on Thursday evening to deliberate on the roadmap for protests over the "vote chori" issue and on ways to press for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation, sources said. Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge will chair the meeting, which will also review the preparations for the INDIA bloc's rally in Delhi on November 1, they said. The INDIA bloc leaders would brainstorm on charting out the roadmap of protests, review the preparations for the November 1 rally and ways to corner the government over the 'vote chori' issue. The meeting also assumes significance as it comes at a time when there is speculation over the government convening Parliament for passing a Constitution amendment bill, involving delimitation, for the early implementation of the Women's Reservation Act. Last week, the protests over the "vote theft" charge reached the Supreme Court's doorstep. On October 12, opposition stalwarts, joined by activists and civil society members, took part in a "March for Democracy" along a heavily barricaded route and filed a joint petition against Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, alleging poll irregularities, in a major show of strength in the national capital. Congress leader Rahul Gandhi also hosted INDIA bloc leaders for tea at his home on October 13. After the meeting, the opposition bloc vowed to continue resisting and take the "vote chori" fight to its logical conclusion.

article_sentences: A landslide near Parassala railway station derailed a locomotive in Kerala, disrupting nine other trains, including the Amrit Bharat Express.
Check details.

A landslide near Parassala railway station in Kerala’s Thiruvananthapuram district derailed the locomotive of the Bilaspur-Tirunelveli Express early Thursday, disrupting services on the Neyyattinkara-Parassala section.
The disruption affected several other trains, including the Tambaram-Thiruvananthapuram Central Amrit Bharat Express.
The incident occurred at 2.19 am when Train No. 22619, the Bilaspur-Tirunelveli Express, was stopped near Parassala following the landslide.
The locomotive was subsequently found to have derailed, Southern Railway said.
All passengers and railway staff are safe, according to the railway authorities.
Three trains were held en route following the incident.
The Tambaram-Thiruvananthapuram Central Special was stopped at Eraniel, the Madurai-Punalur Express at North Panakudi and the Tambaram-Thiruvananthapuram Central Amrit Bharat Express at Nanguneri.
- The Guruvayur-Chennai Egmore Express and the Pune-Kanniyakumari Express were also expected to face delays, Southern Railway said.
Railway authorities arranged a relief locomotive to move the stranded train.
An accident relief train, along with personnel and equipment, was also sent to the site to carry out restoration work and resume services.

stories.headline: Srinagar’s Sprawl is No Mark of Progress
stories.title: Srinagar’s Sprawl is No Mark of Progress
stories.summary: Srinagar is expanding, but it is not growing in the manner a city should. Its boundaries are spreading into villages, agricultural fields, wetlands and open spaces without a coherent urban vision to guide that transformation. What is being celebrated as development increasingly resembles uncontrolled sprawl—a disorderly outward march that is placing immense pressure on land, infrastructure and the environment. The city’s expansion is visible along every major approach road. New colonies, commercial structures and residential complexes are rising rapidly on the outskirts, often ahead of roads, drainage systems, public transport, schools and healthcare facilities. In several areas, construction has become the first sign of urban planning; civic services arrive later, if they arrive at all. This reverses the basic logic of responsible development. Srinagar’s geography makes such expansion particularly dangerous. The city is surrounded by wetlands, water channels, orchards and agricultural land that perform essential ecological functions. These spaces absorb excess water, moderate temperatures and sustain livelihoods. When they are filled, narrowed or built over, the consequences are not limited to the loss of scenery. Flooding becomes more severe, traffic congestion spreads, groundwater systems are disturbed and the city’s capacity to withstand extreme weather declines. The recurring expansion of built-up areas also exposes the weakness of enforcement. Master plans and zoning regulations have little meaning if violations are regularised after construction or if permissions are granted without assessing the cumulative impact on roads, drainage and public utilities. A city cannot be planned plot by plot while ignoring the combined pressure created by thousands of new structures. Urban sprawl also deepens inequality. Affluent developments may create private access roads and independent services, while ordinary residents in peripheral colonies are left with inadequate transport, poor waste collection, unreliable drainage and limited public amenities. The result is a city that becomes larger but not more liveable. Srinagar urgently needs a transparent and enforceable urban growth strategy. Construction on wetlands, flood channels and prime agricultural land must face strict scrutiny. Public transport and compact, mixed-use development should be prioritised over endless low-density expansion. Local bodies must be equipped with updated maps, technical staff and the authority to act against illegal construction—regardless of influence. The question is not whether Srinagar should develop. It must. The question is whether development will serve the city or slowly destroy the conditions that make it habitable. If urban growth continues without ecological restraint and civic planning, Srinagar will inherit the worst features of a metropolis without gaining the benefits of one. Progress cannot mean covering every available piece of land with concrete. A liveable Srinagar must be planned before it is permitted to spread beyond repair.

In several areas, construction has become the first sign of urban planning; civic services arrive later, if they arrive at all.
This reverses the basic logic of responsible development.
Srinagar’s geography makes such expansion particularly dangerous.
The city is surrounded by wetlands, water channels, orchards and agricultural land that perform essential ecological functions.
These spaces absorb excess water, moderate temperatures and sustain livelihoods.
When they are filled, narrowed or built over, the consequences are not limited to the loss of scenery.
Flooding becomes more severe, traffic congestion spreads, groundwater systems are disturbed and the city’s capacity to withstand extreme weather declines.
The recurring expansion of built-up areas also exposes the weakness of enforcement.

Master plans and zoning regulations have little meaning if violations are regularised after construction or if permissions are granted without assessing the cumulative impact on roads, drainage and public utilities.
A city cannot be planned plot by plot while ignoring the combined pressure created by thousands of new structures.
Urban sprawl also deepens inequality.

Affluent developments may create private access roads and independent services, while ordinary residents in peripheral colonies are left with inadequate transport, poor waste collection, unreliable drainage and limited public amenities.
The result is a city that becomes larger but not more liveable.
Srinagar urgently needs a transparent and enforceable urban growth strategy.
Construction on wetlands, flood channels and prime agricultural land must face strict scrutiny.
Public transport and compact, mixed-use development should be prioritised over endless low-density expansion.
Local bodies must be equipped with updated maps, technical staff and the authority to act against illegal construction—regardless of influence.
The question is not whether Srinagar should develop.
It must.
The question is whether development will serve the city or slowly destroy the conditions that make it habitable.
If urban growth continues without ecological restraint and civic planning, Srinagar will inherit the worst features of a metropolis without gaining the benefits of one.
Progress cannot mean covering every available piece of land with concrete.
A liveable Srinagar must be planned before it is permitted to spread beyond repair.

stories.headline: Div Com reviews alignment of Srinagar Ring Road Phase-III, Parimpora–Dalgate Flyover
stories.title: Div Com reviews alignment of Srinagar Ring Road Phase-III, Parimpora–Dalgate Flyover
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 21: Divisional Commissioner Kashmir, Anshul Garg on Wednesday chaired a meeting of officers to review the cahnge in proposed realignments of Srinagar Ring Road Phase-III (Lasjan–Pandach) and the Parimpora–Dalgate Flyover. The meeting was attended by the Commissioner, Srinagar Municipal Corporation (SMC); Deputy Commissioner Srinagar; SSP Traffic; Vice Chairman, Lakes Conservation and Management Authority (LCMA); Project Director, National Highways Authority of India (NHAI); and officers from the Roads and Buildings (R&B) Department, Irrigation and Flood Control Department, Srinagar Development Authority (SDA), and other concerned departments. During the review of Srinagar Ring Road Phase-III (Lasjan–Pandach), the Divisional Commissioner directed NHAI officials to compile comprehensive details of structures and departmental utilities falling within the proposed alignments including religious structures to access impediments & challenges and cost expenditure. He further directed the concerned authorities to explore modifications to the alignment to ensure that the road does not encroach upon the city's major water body. Reviewing the proposed alignment of the Parimpora–Dalgate Flyover, the Divisional Commissioner directed the R&B Department to explore an alternative alignments from Qamarwari to Nalamar and onward to Karanagar. He emphasized the need to ensure connectivity to key facilities, including SMHS Hospital, while minimizing traffic disruptions during the execution of the project. The concerned departments were directed to examine the proposed alignments in coordination with one another, keeping public convenience and essential infrastructure.
